analysis.one_liner: Gives part-time workers equal pay and benefits, first claim on extra hours, and shorter-tenure family leave.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or hearing; it sat in the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten two basic rules for part-time and temporary workers. First, it would have let workers take unpaid, job-protected family and medical leave after 90 days on the job instead of the current 12 months and 1,250 hours worked [S2]. Second, it would have barred employers from paying part-time and temporary workers less than full-time workers doing the same work, or denying them benefits, promotions, and a say in their schedules, and would have required employers to offer extra hours to current part-time workers before hiring anyone new, paying current workers for hours a new hire takes [S2]. The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken on it [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Part-time and temporary workers gain directly: equal pay for substantially equal work, pro rata access to paid and unpaid time off and benefits, promotion opportunities, notice of and input into their hours, and a legal right to be offered extra hours before an employer hires new staff or brings in a temp agency — backed by private lawsuits with doubled damages and Labor Department enforcement [S2]. Workers would also qualify for family and medical leave after 90 days rather than after a year and 1,250 hours, which currently screens out many part-timers [S2]. The bill's own text applies these rights to private employees, federal and congressional employees, and state employees covered by the Government Employee Rights Act [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Lets employees take job-protected family and medical leave after 90 days of employment instead of the current requirement of 12 months of service and 1,250 hours worked, a threshold that excludes most part-time workers, and applies the same change to congressional and federal employees [S2].

Makes it illegal to pay part-time or temporary workers less than full-time workers with substantially equal skill, effort, and duties, or to deny them pro rata benefits, promotions, or input into their schedules because of their hours [S2].

Requires employers to collect each worker's desired weekly hours at hire and to offer open hours to existing employees before hiring new workers or staffing agencies, and to compensate existing workers for hours that a new hire works during the existing employee's stated availability — a check on unpredictable, under-scheduled work [S2].

Gives workers real enforcement: private lawsuits including class actions, doubled (liquidated) damages plus interest, attorney's fees, reinstatement or promotion, and Labor Department investigations with civil penalties from $500 to $5,000 per willful violation, adjusted for inflation [S2].

Counts franchises and integrated chains in the aggregate toward the 15-employee coverage threshold, so a franchisor cannot divide itself into small stores to dodge the law, and bars retaliation against workers who assert these rights [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear the cost: businesses would have to equalize pay and benefits between part-time and full-time staff, offer hours to current workers before hiring, and pay damages to workers for violations. The bill covers any employer in commerce with more than 15 employees, counting all part-time and temporary staff, and counts franchise chains in the aggregate, which reaches many retail, restaurant, and franchise operations [S2]. The FMLA expansion would increase the number of employees entitled to 12 weeks of protected leave [S2]. Taxpayers do not fund any part of the bill; it relies on employer compliance and worker lawsuits [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Retail, restaurant, franchise, and staffing employers

drawbacks.text: The costs fall on businesses that employ many part-time workers. Equalizing pay and benefits between part-time and full-time staff, plus compensating existing employees for hours new hires work, would raise labor costs for retail, restaurant, and franchise employers — costs that could surface as higher prices, fewer new part-time positions, or pressure to convert part-time jobs to full-time or automation [S2].

The franchise-counting rule pulls entire chains into coverage even where a single store has only a handful of employees, and the 15-employee threshold applies the same scheduling and pay rules to relatively small businesses, which have the least compliance capacity [S2].

Dropping the FMLA requirement from 12 months and 1,250 hours to just 90 days — with no minimum hours at all — would entitle a worker to 12 weeks of protected leave less than three months into a job, and the bill provides no employee-side cost-sharing or transition period beyond one year, which supporters' critics would say raises hiring risk for employers and could make them wary of new hires [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions of Americans working part-time, the benefits are substantial and direct: equal pay, pro rata benefits, predictable hours, and family leave after 90 days [S2]. The costs are real but conventional — they are the compliance and wage costs of extending full-time workplace standards to part-time staff, the same trade-off every wage-and-hours law makes, and the bill includes a good-faith exception that lets courts reduce doubled damages [S2]. The strongest design criticism is the 90-day, zero-hours FMLA threshold, which is far more generous than the federal standard or any state analogue and would impose leave obligations on employers almost immediately after hire; a phased or minimum-hours approach would have blunted that objection. On balance, the bill is a straightforward transfer of workplace protections to a group that currently has few.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to its labor committee the day it was introduced in September 2023, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Warren introduced the Part-Time Worker Bill of Rights Act with eight cosponsors — Senators Sanders, Whitehouse, Markey, Casey, Booker, Welch, Murray, and Padilla — on September 19, 2023 [S1][S3].
That same day the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S4].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote followed; the full action history shows no action after the referral for the rest of the 118th Congress [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and bills not passed die at the end of a Congress, so the bill is dead unless reintroduced [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of large part-time workforces — retail, restaurant, and franchise chains and staffing agencies — are better off, because they keep the current rules that allow paying part-timers less, offering fewer benefits, and hiring new staff instead of giving existing workers hours. The bill's sponsors are not better off; they gained no policy change.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its advocacy as its Senate sponsor

for.name: Sens. Sanders, Whitehouse, Markey, Casey, Booker, Welch, Murray, and Padilla
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the only senators to support it on the record

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the entire 118th Congress; the action history shows no committee action after the referral

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; it could not be scheduled because it never cleared committee

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no roll-call split exists; all nine known supporters were Democrats plus one Independent, and no Republican sponsored or publicly backed the bill in the record.

industries.note: These employers rely on large part-time workforces and would have had to equalize pay and benefits, offer existing workers extra hours before hiring, and pay for under-scheduling. Their interest in keeping the status quo runs directly against the part-time workers the bill covers.

The bill requires employers to exhaust their own workers' stated availability before using a staffing agency or subcontractor, and counts agency-supplied workers in coverage calculations — shrinking the market for temp labor placement.

The bill counts franchise networks and integrated chains in the aggregate toward the 15-employee threshold, closing the common practice of structuring each location as a small employer to avoid coverage.
The bill extends the same rights to congressional staff, federal employees, GAO staff, and covered state employees, with their existing internal enforcement boards handling complaints.
